transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I'm here because I spend so much time checking and rechecking how I look at the gym and before going out that it’s taking over my days. It has just become really exhausting to deal with.
When you're checking how you look, do you feel driven to do it because of persistent thoughts that something is wrong with your appearance, even if you don't want to?

Yes, absolutely. I'm constantly plagued by thoughts about how crooked my face looks and how weird my jawline is from the side. Even though I don't want to waste time, I feel completely compelled to spend hours checking mirrors, fixing my hair and clothes, and zooming in on photos to try and hide it.
Do you ever think that these concerns about your appearance might be excessive or not completely true, even though the urge to check still feels strong?

I haven't really thought about it that way because the flaws feel so incredibly real to me when I look in the mirror. It's hard to believe it might be excessive when my crooked face and jawline just look so obviously wrong to me.
Have you ever considered that these appearance concerns might not be as noticeable to others, or that they might be part of a mental health condition rather than actual physical flaws?

My friends keep telling me they don't see anything wrong, and my sister actually urged me to see a professional, which is why I'm here today. But it's just so hard to believe them because when I look at photos or in the mirror, my crooked face and weird jawline feel completely real and obvious to me.
Even though you feel these appearance concerns strongly, have you ever been able to step back and recognize that they might be influenced by your thoughts rather than actual flaws?
I'm not really sure, and I haven't ever thought about it that way. To me, the flaws feel completely real when I look in the mirror, so it's hard to believe it's just my thoughts.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F42, F63.3], but based on this conversation, F42 (obsessive-compulsive disorder) seems less likely because the patient's preoccupation with facial asymmetry and jawline is tied to a distorted perception of appearance that feels subjectively real, despite reassurance from others. The lack of insight—specifically the inability to recognize that the concerns may be related to a mental condition—aligns more closely with body dysmorphic disorder (F63.3). The compulsive checking behaviors are present, but they stem from a delusional or near-delusional belief in the reality of the flaw, which is characteristic of F63.3 rather than typical OCD presentations under F42.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent and intrusive preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance (facial asymmetry and jawline), leading to compulsive checking behaviors. Despite reassurance from others, the patient has poor insight, believing the flaws are objectively obvious, which aligns with body dysmorphic disorder. The symptoms cause significant time consumption and distress, meeting diagnostic criteria.
